section.title: The Seventy-Two and the Good Samaritan
section.sectionRationale: As the journey to Jerusalem unfolds, Jesus widens the mission by sending seventy-two ahead of Him, then teaches them to rejoice not in power but in grace. He praises the Father for revealing the kingdom to little children, answers a lawyer's test with the parable of the Good Samaritan, and ends in a home where Mary chooses the one necessary thing. Mission, mercy, and attentive love to the Lord belong together.
section.thesis: The kingdom advances through humble sent messengers who rejoice that their names are written in heaven, it bends down in costly mercy to the half-dead stranger, and it is received above all by those who sit at Jesus' feet and choose the one thing needful.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the sending and warning of the seventy-two; their joyful return and Jesus' thanksgiving; the parable of the Good Samaritan; and Martha and Mary and the one necessary thing.

verses.text: After this, the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them two by two ahead of Him to every town and place He was about to visit.
And He told them, “The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest.
Go! I am sending you out like lambs among wolves.
Carry no purse or bag or sandals. Do not greet anyone along the road.
Whatever house you enter, begin by saying, ‘Peace to this house.’
If a man of peace is there, your peace will rest on him; if not, it will return to you.
Stay at the same house, eating and drinking whatever you are offered. For the worker is worthy of his wages. Do not move around from house to house.
If you enter a town and they welcome you, eat whatever is set before you.
Heal the sick who are there and tell them, ‘The kingdom of God is near you.’
But if you enter a town and they do not welcome you, go into the streets and declare,
‘Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet, we wipe off as a testimony against you. Yet be sure of this: The kingdom of God is near.’
I tell you, it will be more bearable on that day for Sodom than for that town.
Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes.
But it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon at the judgment than for you.
And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up to heaven? No, you will be brought down to Hades!
Whoever listens to you listens to Me; whoever rejects you rejects Me; and whoever rejects Me rejects the One who sent Me.”

units.label: The joyful return and Jesus' thanksgiving
units.note: rejoice that your names are written in heaven

verses.text: The seventy-two returned with {{chara|joy}} and said, “Lord, even the demons submit to us in Your name.”
So He told them, “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.
Behold, I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. Nothing will harm you.
Nevertheless, do not rejoice that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.”

At that time Jesus rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and declared, “I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, for this was well-pleasing in Your sight.
All things have been entrusted to Me by My Father. No one knows who the Son is except the Father, and no one knows who the Father is except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.”
Then Jesus turned to the disciples and said privately, “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see.
For I tell you that many prophets and kings desired to see what you see but did not see it, and to hear what you hear but did not hear it.”
One day an expert in the law stood up to test Him. “Teacher,” he asked, “what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
“What is written in the Law?” Jesus replied. “How do you read it?”
He answered, “‘{{agapao|Love}} the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind’ and ‘Love your {{plesion|neighbor}} as yourself.’”
“You have answered correctly,” Jesus said. “Do this and you will live.”
But wanting to justify himself, he asked Jesus, “And who is my {{plesion|neighbor}}?”
Jesus took up this question and said, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho when he fell into the hands of robbers. They stripped him, beat him, and went away, leaving him half dead.
Now by chance a priest was going down the same road, but when he saw him, he passed by on the other side.
So too, when a Levite came to that spot and saw him, he passed by on the other side.
But a Samaritan on a journey came upon him, and when he saw him, he {{splanchnizomai|had compassion}}.
He went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he put him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
The next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper. ‘Take care of him,’ he said, ‘and on my return I will repay you for any additional expense.’
Which of these three do you think was a {{plesion|neighbor}} to the man who fell into the hands of robbers?”
“The one who showed him mercy,” replied the expert in the law. Then Jesus told him, “Go and do likewise.”
As they traveled along, Jesus entered a village where a woman named Martha welcomed Him into her home.
She had a sister named Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet listening to His message.
But Martha was distracted by all the preparations to be made. She came to Jesus and said, “Lord, do You not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her to help me!”
“Martha, Martha,” the Lord replied, “you are worried and upset about many things.
But only one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, and it will not be taken away from her.”

chara.gloss: Joy, gladness. The seventy-two return with joy over their authority, but Jesus redirects the deeper joy to a surer ground: that their names are written in heaven. Gospel joy rests finally on grace received, not on results achieved.

agapao.gloss: To love with the will and in action, to seek another's good. The great commandment gathers up the whole law: to love God wholly and the neighbor as oneself. The parable then shows that such love is measured not in words but in costly mercy.

plesion.gloss: Neighbor, the one near at hand. The lawyer tries to narrow who counts as neighbor; Jesus reverses the question, so that being a neighbor means becoming one to whoever lies in need, even a despised stranger.

splanchnizomai.gloss: To be moved with compassion in the depths, a gut-level mercy. The same verb describes Jesus' own heart for the crowds and the father's welcome of the prodigal. Here it moves the Samaritan to cross the road and pay the price of another's rescue.

basic.context: On the way to Jerusalem Jesus sends out seventy-two workers ahead of Him with the message that the kingdom of God is near. They return thrilled that even demons obeyed, and Jesus teaches them to rejoice instead that their names are written in heaven. He thanks the Father for revealing the kingdom to little children. Then a lawyer tests Him about eternal life, and Jesus answers his self-justifying question, who is my neighbor, with the story of a Samaritan who shows mercy where a priest and a Levite would not. Finally, in Martha's home, Mary sits at Jesus' feet, and Jesus says she has chosen the one thing that cannot be taken away.
basic.hermeneutics: Hold the three scenes together. The mission is urgent but its true joy is grace, not success. The parable is not a tidy lesson in being nice; it explodes the lawyer's attempt to limit love and demands mercy toward the outsider. And Martha and Mary guard the whole against activism: even good service must flow from sitting at Jesus' feet and hearing His word.
basic.originalLanguages: The seventy-two return with chara, joy, which Jesus anchors in heaven rather than in power. The lawyer cites the command to agapao, to love, God and neighbor, plesion. The turning point of the parable is splanchnizomai, gut-deep compassion, the very mercy that moves the heart of God.
basic.typology: The Samaritan who finds the half-dead man, binds his wounds, pays his debt, and promises to return has long been heard as an image of Christ Himself, who comes to the ruined and rescues at His own cost. The good portion Mary chooses is the Word made flesh, present and speaking.
basic.christ: Jesus is the sender of the harvest workers and the one in whom the kingdom draws near. He is the Son who alone knows and reveals the Father. In the parable He both commands mercy and embodies it, the true neighbor who crosses every barrier to save. And He is the one necessary thing at whose feet Mary sits.
basic.god: The Father is Lord of heaven and earth, who hides the kingdom from the self-sufficient and reveals it to little children according to His good pleasure. He is the God whose mercy the parable mirrors and whose Son is the harvest's Lord.
basic.crossReferences: Leviticus 19 and Deuteronomy 6 supply the great commandment. Matthew 9 shows Jesus moved with the same compassion for the harvest crowds. James 2 insists that love without deeds is dead. Philippians 3 counts all things loss for the one thing of knowing Christ.
basic.oneStory: The kingdom advances through humble sent workers, bends down in costly mercy to the outsider, and is received by those who sit and listen at Jesus' feet. In the merciful Samaritan we glimpse the Lord who rescues us, and in Mary we see the heart that treasures Him above all.

context.literary:
The chapter opens with 'After this' and so reads as the answer to what Luke has just reported. In Luke 9:51-56 Jesus set His face toward Jerusalem and sent messengers ahead into a Samaritan village that would not receive Him, and James and John wanted to call down fire. Chapter 10 returns to the road with a wider mission and ends up with a Samaritan as the hero of the best-known parable in the Gospels. The placement is deliberate, and the reader is meant to feel the correction.

The chapter falls into five movements, each a pair of verbs of hearing and doing. The sending in verses 1 to 16 closes on a statement about listening: 'Whoever listens to you listens to Me.' The return in verses 17 to 20 and the thanksgiving in verses 21 to 24 turn the same ears toward what is truly worth hearing and seeing. The lawyer's scene in verses 25 to 37 is built on doing, 'do this and you will live,' answered by 'Go and do likewise.' Martha and Mary in verses 38 to 42 return to listening: Mary 'sat at the Lord's feet listening to His message.' Doing and hearing hold each other in place, and the order matters, because the final scene puts hearing first.

The parable is told with great economy. Priest, Levite and Samaritan all 'see' the wounded man, and the verb is the same for each. The difference lies entirely in what follows the seeing: a detour for the first two, and for the third a stopping, a touching and a spending. The story also leaves the victim unnamed and without identity, so that no reader can decide who deserves help before the helping begins. Jesus then turns the lawyer's question around. The lawyer asked who counts as his neighbor; Jesus asks who proved to be one, verse 36.
context.historical:
Jesus sends the seventy-two ahead 'to every town and place He was about to visit,' verse 1, so they are advance parties, not independent missionaries, and their instructions fit the speed of that work. Carrying no purse or bag, and greeting no one on the road, recalls Elisha's instruction to Gehazi in 2 Kings 4:29, when the errand was too urgent for the courtesies that could take half a day. The Lord of the harvest sends them to households first, and the greeting of peace is the ordinary Jewish blessing, which Jesus charges with the substance of the kingdom: the peace rests on a 'man of peace,' or comes back to the sender.

The number carries echoes. Moses took seventy elders up the mountain in Exodus 24:1 and God shared the Spirit that was on him with seventy elders in Numbers 11:16-25. The Hebrew text of Genesis 10 is commonly counted as listing seventy nations, and the early Greek translation as seventy-two. Luke does not say which he means, and the echo of the elders and the echo of the nations both fit a Jesus who is reconstituting Israel and reaching beyond her.

The parable depends on a map and on a feud. The road from Jerusalem to Jericho runs roughly seventeen miles and drops well over three thousand feet, through rocky wilderness that gave robbers every hiding place. A priest and a Levite travelling down from Jerusalem are likely coming away from their Temple service. Leviticus 21:1-3 forbids a priest to defile himself for a dead person except for close family, so some hearers would have supplied a purity excuse for the priest. Jesus does not offer one, and the half-dead man was not yet a corpse. The Samaritans, descendants of the northern kingdom's mixed population, 2 Kings 17:24, worshipped on Mount Gerizim and accepted only the first five books of Moses. John 4:9 sums up the relationship: 'Jews do not associate with Samaritans.' In John 8:48 'Samaritan' is hurled at Jesus as an insult, joined to the charge of having a demon. A Samaritan on the Jericho road would have sounded like the villain, and the lawyer cannot bring himself to say the word in verse 37, answering only 'The one who showed him mercy.' Two denarii, verse 35, were about two days' wages for a labourer, Matthew 20:2, enough to keep a lodger for some time.
context.canonical:
Three Old Testament texts stand behind the lawyer's exchange. Deuteronomy 6:5 supplies the first command, though Luke's lawyer adds 'with all your mind' to the three terms of the Hebrew. Leviticus 19:18 supplies the second, and its setting matters, because the same chapter says in verse 34 that the foreigner living among you is to be loved 'as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.' Jesus' answer to 'who is my neighbor' is therefore a reading of Leviticus 19 as a whole. 'Do this and you will live' echoes Leviticus 18:5, a verse Paul later sets beside faith in Galatians 3:12 and Romans 10:5 to show that the law promises life to perfect doing and that no one has done it.

There is also a remarkable earlier story. In 2 Chronicles 28:8-15 men of Samaria take Judean captives, hear a prophet's rebuke, and then clothe the naked, give them food and drink, anoint their wounds, put the feeble on donkeys and bring them to Jericho. Whether or not Jesus had that account in mind, the details match, and the Old Testament already knew that Samaria could show Judah mercy.

The chapter's other threads run forward. The names 'written in heaven,' verse 20, recall the book of Exodus 32:32 and Daniel 12:1 and arrive at the Lamb's book of life in Revelation 21:27. The Father and Son's mutual knowledge in verse 22 reappears in John 10:15 and 17:25. Luke himself follows the Samaritan thread: a Samaritan leper returns to give thanks in Luke 17:11-19, and in Acts 8 Samaria receives the word through Philip and then Peter and John, who are the same pair who once wanted fire for Samaria, Acts 8:14-17.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke tells this chapter to disciples who will themselves be sent, and he wants three things settled in them. First, the mission is the Lord's before it is theirs. They are asked to pray for workers before they are told to go, verse 2, and they return to hear that their success came from Jesus' own victory over Satan, verse 18, not from their personal power. Second, knowing the law is not the same as keeping it. The lawyer answers his own question correctly and still needs the parable, because he is trying to arrange the commandment so that it asks less of him than it does. Luke gives no verdict on his later response, and the story simply ends on the command 'Go and do likewise.' Third, Luke wants active service held under a prior act of listening. Martha is not shown to be wicked, but she is shown to be anxious about many things while Mary has taken hold of the one thing the whole chapter has been pointing to, which is the Lord's word.

The first hearers of the parable would have recognised the road and the three travellers. They were meant to feel the shock of the third, and then to find in that shock the verdict on their own habits of sorting people into those who count and those who do not.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The detailed instructions to the seventy-two are descriptive of one short mission. Carrying no purse or sandals, greeting no one, and staying in a single house were tied to the speed of an advance party sent into towns Jesus Himself was about to enter. Later Jesus tells the same disciples to take purse and bag in Luke 22:35-36, which shows that the equipment changed with the circumstances. What stays in force is the pattern: pray for workers, go as those who are sent, offer peace, accept support, announce that the kingdom is near, and leave judgment to the Lord.

The parable is different. It ends with an imperative, 'Go and do likewise,' so its main point is prescriptive for every reader. It does not set out a program for social work, and it does not need to, because it shows what mercy looks like when it costs time, money and risk, and it forbids any use of the neighbor question as a reason to stop. The Martha and Mary scene describes a single visit, and the verdict is about priority, not about whether meals should be served. Read together with Luke 8:21 and 11:28, it shows that hearing the word of God and doing it is what Jesus values most.

debates.question: Is the Good Samaritan mainly a call to love or a picture of Christ?

views.label: A call to merciful love
views.case: In its setting the parable answers who is my neighbor and ends with go and do likewise, pressing every hearer to costly mercy toward whoever is in need, even an enemy.

views.label: A picture of Christ the rescuer
views.case: Many read the Samaritan, the despised outsider who saves the half-dead man at his own cost and promises to return, as an image of Jesus who comes to the ruined and pays for their healing.

debates.bearing: The primary thrust is the command to show mercy, yet the mercy commanded is precisely the mercy Christ shows us, so the two readings reinforce rather than cancel each other.

debates.question: Does the praise of Mary devalue Martha's service?

views.label: Listening must come first
views.case: Jesus gently corrects not Martha's serving but her anxious distraction; Mary has chosen the one necessary thing, hearing His word, from which true service flows.

views.label: A rebuke of hospitality
views.case: Some hear it as downgrading practical service, but the context, a welcomed guest and an anxious host, shows the issue is worried, self-important busyness that crowds out attention to the Lord.

debates.bearing: Service is good, but it must be rooted in and never replace attentive love to Jesus; Mary's good portion is the wellspring, not the enemy, of faithful work.

debates.question: Did Jesus send seventy or seventy-two?

views.label: Seventy-two
views.case: The BSB follows the early manuscripts that read seventy-two in verses 1 and 17. Some of the oldest witnesses support it, and a scribe who knew the round number seventy from Exodus 24:1 and Numbers 11:16 would have had a reason to smooth seventy-two into it, which makes the odder number the more likely original.

views.label: Seventy
views.case: The BSB footnote notes that other manuscript traditions read seventy in both verses. The round number lines up with the seventy elders of Moses and with the commonly counted seventy nations of the Hebrew text of Genesis 10, and a scribe might equally have wanted that symbolism.

debates.bearing: The two readings differ by two people, and every symbolic echo, whether Moses' elders or the nations, points the same way: this is a mission that reaches beyond the Twelve and, in the end, beyond Israel. Nothing in the teaching depends on settling the count.

study.originalLanguages:
Several small words in this chapter carry weight that the English smooths over. In verse 2 Jesus asks the disciples to pray that the Lord of the harvest will 'send out' workers, and the Greek verb is ekballo, a strong word that literally means to throw or drive out, the same verb used of casting out demons. The picture is of workers who will not leave their comforts unless God thrusts them into the field. The same stress belongs to the announcement in verses 9 and 11, 'the kingdom of God is near you.' The verb engiken is in the perfect tense: the kingdom has drawn near and stands near. Jesus tells them to say this even in the town that rejects them, so the nearness is a fact that does not depend on the town's reception.

Verse 20 tells the disciples to rejoice that their names 'are written in heaven.' The verb is again perfect, eggegraptai, meaning that they have been written and the record stands. The ground of joy is a finished act, set against the passing triumph over demons. A few verses later Jesus 'rejoiced in the Holy Spirit,' verse 21, using egalliasato, a strong and exultant verb that Luke uses of Mary's song in Luke 1:47. It is the language of worship, and it shows that Jesus' own joy is Trinitarian: He rejoices in the Spirit as He thanks the Father about the Son.

The heart of the parable lies in two words. In verse 29 the lawyer asks who is his neighbor, plesion, the Greek word the Septuagint uses for the Hebrew of Leviticus 19:18. Jesus' question in verse 36 does not ask who is the neighbor but which of the three 'proved to be a neighbor,' using the verb ginomai, to become. Neighborliness becomes something a person does, not a category into which others fall. Verse 33 then names the Samaritan's inner movement with esplanchnisthe, from splanchna, the inner organs regarded as the seat of feeling. Luke uses this verb of Jesus at the widow's funeral in Luke 7:13, of the Samaritan here, and of the waiting father in Luke 15:20, which makes it his word for the compassion that precedes rescue. The lawyer's own description of the Samaritan in verse 37 is literally 'the one who did mercy with him,' and the phrase echoes the Hebrew idiom of doing kindness, as in Genesis 24:12.

Finally, in verse 40 Martha is 'distracted,' a word from perispao that pictures being pulled about in several directions at once, and Jesus names her state with merimnas, 'worried,' adding that she is upset about many things. The 'good portion' of verse 42 uses the language of a share that is allotted, and the promise that it 'will not be taken away' answers Martha's fear that the work is being taken from her hands.

typology.type: The seventy elders and the Spirit, Numbers 11:16-25
typology.fulfillment: Moses was overburdened, and God took of the Spirit on him and put it on seventy elders, who prophesied. When Joshua wanted two who prophesied in the camp stopped, Moses answered, 'I wish that all the LORD's people were prophets,' Numbers 11:29. Jesus appoints seventy-two others beyond the Twelve, and the longing of Moses starts to come true, until at Pentecost the Spirit is poured out on all who believe, Acts 2:17-18. The type falls short in that the elders served one leader in one camp, whereas Christ gives His Spirit and sends His people to every nation, Acts 1:8.

typology.type: The Samaritan who finds, binds and pays, Luke 10:33-35
typology.fulfillment: The parable is first a command, but its details have long reminded readers of Christ. A despised outsider stops where the respectable pass by, binds wounds with oil and wine, bears the man on his own animal, pays the price and promises to return. The Lord is the one who 'heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds,' Psalm 147:3, and Isaiah 53:3 describes Him as 'despised and rejected by men.' The correspondence is real, but it is not the parable's main point, and the escalation in Christ is that He paid not two denarii but His life, 1 Peter 2:24, and the return He promises is the one Luke 12 awaits.

typology.type: Names written in the book, Exodus 32:32 and Daniel 12:1
typology.fulfillment: Moses once asked to be blotted out of God's book in place of a sinful people, and Daniel looked ahead to the day when everyone 'found written in the book' would be delivered. Jesus tells the seventy-two that their names are already written in heaven, and Revelation 21:27 names the book as 'the Lamb's book of life.' The roll is secured by the Lamb who was slain, Revelation 13:8, and not by the achievements of those listed. Moses' offer could not be accepted, Exodus 32:33, but Christ's can, and that is why the disciples' joy rests on something no demon can reach.

typology.type: The Word chosen over bread, Luke 10:42 and Deuteronomy 8:3
typology.fulfillment: When Israel was fed in the wilderness, Moses taught that a person does not live by bread alone but by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD, Deuteronomy 8:3, and Jesus quoted that line against the devil, Luke 4:4. Mary's choice in a kitchen household puts the same priority into action: the word of the Lord is the portion that sustains. In Christ the correspondence deepens, because He is Himself the Word who became flesh, John 1:14, and the one sitting in the room. The type falls short if hearing is separated from doing, and Luke 11:28 and James 1:22 join them.

study.christ:
The chapter shows Christ in four distinct postures, and each is tied to a text in Luke or elsewhere in the New Testament. First, He is the Lord of the harvest in whose name others go. The workers are to 'ask the Lord of the harvest,' yet the one who sends them is Jesus, verse 1, and in verse 16 He puts His own person where the message is: whoever rejects them rejects Him, and whoever rejects Him rejects the One who sent Him. That is a claim to stand in the place of God, and Luke's hearers would have known it.

Second, He is the conqueror of Satan. 'I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven' in verse 18 is spoken in the past tense by one who watched it happen, and it fits the picture in John 12:31 and Revelation 12:9-10. The authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, verse 19, is His to give, and Psalm 91:13 had promised that the one who dwells in God's shelter would tread on lion and cobra. In Luke 4:1-13 Jesus Himself met the devil and won; now His people share the victory by His name.

Third, He is the gatekeeper of the knowledge of God. Verse 22 is the nearest Luke comes to the voice of John's Gospel: all things have been handed over to Him, and no one finds the Father by cleverness, only by the Son's own choosing. This is why the 'wise and learned' fail and the 'little children' receive, and why even the prophets and kings who longed to see Messiah's day were envied by the disciples, verses 23 and 24.

Fourth, in the parable and the scene at Bethany He is both the example of mercy and the one worth listening to. The Samaritan resembles Him, though the parable's weight lies elsewhere, and any claim that the parable is an allegory of the gospel should be made with caution. What can safely be said is that the lawyer's question, what must I do to inherit eternal life, receives from the law the answer 'do this and live,' and that the one who tells the story is the only person who has done it. Mary, finally, sits at the feet of the one Luke calls 'the Lord' in verse 39, and her portion is Himself.
study.god:
The chapter gives a vivid view of God as sender, as Father and as the one who shows mercy. He is the Lord of the harvest, and the harvest belongs to Him. The disciples' first act is to pray, and their first discovery is that the work outruns their number. God is not short of power, but He chooses to work through the sent, and He tells them to expect rejection and to remain at peace, because rejection of the messenger is finally rejection of Him, verse 16.

Verses 21 and 22 are among the richest passages in Luke on the doctrine of God. Jesus rejoices 'in the Holy Spirit' and addresses the Father as 'Lord of heaven and earth,' while speaking of Himself as the Son to whom all things are entrusted. Father, Son and Spirit are all active in a single moment of praise. The Father's sovereignty is also stated plainly: He has hidden these things from the wise and learned and revealed them to little children, and this was 'well-pleasing in Your sight.' Luke does not explain how the hiding and revealing fit with human responsibility, and the chapter does not need to, because the same Lord has just sent the messengers into every town, and the towns that refuse will be judged for refusing, verses 12 to 15. Divine initiative and human accountability sit side by side.

The chapter also shows God as just and measured. Sodom, Tyre and Sidon will find it 'more bearable' than the towns that saw Jesus' miracles, so judgment is weighed against the light received. God is not careless of the many who have not heard, and He is not indifferent to those who have heard and shrugged.

Finally, the parable mirrors what God is like by commanding what He is. Mercy that sees and then crosses the road, that pays and promises to return, is the way God treats those who are fallen. In worship this chapter teaches us to be glad first that we belong to Him, and to measure our lives by whether we hear Him and whether we have crossed the road.

crossReferences.note: The scene just before. A Samaritan village refuses Jesus, and James and John want to call down fire. Chapter 10 reverses that hostility, first by sending a wider mission and then by making a Samaritan the model of neighbor love. Reading the two together shows the parable was not a decorative story but a reply to a live prejudice among Jesus' own followers.

God takes of the Spirit that was on Moses and places it on seventy elders. The echo with the seventy sent by Jesus suggests a new company of Spirit-filled helpers, and Moses' wish in verse 29 that all God's people were prophets begins to move toward fulfillment.

Elisha tells Gehazi not to greet anyone on the way, because the errand cannot wait. Jesus gives the same urgent instruction in verse 4. The comparison shows the instruction is about speed and focus, and it was never a rule about etiquette for all missionaries.

The neighbor command in its own setting sits among laws against hatred and revenge between fellow Israelites. The lawyer is therefore right to quote it, and Jesus is not changing the law but exposing the narrowing of its scope that the lawyer's follow-up question assumes.

Just sixteen verses on in the same chapter, the foreigner living among Israel is to be treated as native-born and loved 'as yourself.' This is the text that makes the Samaritan fit the law's own horizon. A neighbor is not limited by blood or by religion.

Men from Samaria clothe, feed, anoint and carry Judean captives on donkeys, and bring them to Jericho. The parallels with the parable are so close that many readers suspect Jesus drew on it. Even if He did not, it shows that the Scriptures already told of mercy crossing that same ethnic line.

Matthew places the same thanksgiving to the Father and the same statement about the Son's unique knowledge in a different setting. The parallel confirms that the saying belongs to the tradition of Jesus' own words and not to a single Gospel's theology, and it shows that the passage had a lasting life in the early church.

Paul quotes 'The worker is worthy of his wages' as Scripture, setting it beside Deuteronomy 25:4. That is the saying of Luke 10:7, which shows the early church treated words of Jesus preserved in Luke as carrying the authority of Scripture, and that the principle of supporting workers survived the end of the seventy-two's mission.

The one who makes the LORD his refuge will tread on lion and cobra. Jesus' promise in verse 19 that His messengers will tread on snakes and scorpions uses the same picture of victory over dangerous creatures, and applies it to the powers of darkness. Satan himself quoted Psalm 91 to tempt Jesus in Luke 4:10-11, and here the Lord shows what it truly means.

John names the village as Bethany and calls Martha and Mary sisters of Lazarus. Luke leaves the village unnamed, but John shows the same two women in the same roles: Martha comes to meet Jesus with a confession in John 11:20-27, and Mary again sits at His feet in John 11:32 and 12:3. The Luke scene is therefore a snapshot of a settled friendship.

Peter and John, who once wanted to burn a Samaritan village, now travel to Samaria to pray that the new believers may receive the Holy Spirit. The Jericho road parable is finally answered in the church's own history, and Luke has arranged his two volumes so that readers can see it.

study.oneStory:
The chapter sits where the story of Scripture turns from Israel to the nations. Genesis 10 listed the families of the earth after the flood, and Genesis 12:3 promised that all of them would be blessed in Abraham. Through Israel's long history that promise was often forgotten, as when Jonah resented Nineveh and the Jews of Jesus' day resented Samaria. Here the Lord of the harvest sends the first workers, in advance parties, to every place He is about to visit, and the line from Genesis 10 begins to be traced in reverse.

The chapter also answers a question the law raised and could not answer. Leviticus 18:5 held out life to the one who does the commandments, and Deuteronomy 6 and Leviticus 19 summarised them as love for God and neighbor. The lawyer is right about the content and wrong about his own power, and the story of the Samaritan shows how far the demand goes. After the fall the human heart does not naturally cross the road. The gospel is therefore not a lesser demand but the gift of a new heart, and that is why the disciples are told to rejoice that their names are written, not that they have succeeded.

The story's flow forward is equally clear. Satan's fall in verse 18 is the first sign of the defeat that Revelation 12:9 describes in full, and the book of names in verse 20 anticipates the Lamb's book of life at the end. The scene at Martha's house points to the day when God's people will no longer be pulled in many directions but will sit at His feet, and Revelation 22:3-4 says His servants will serve Him and see His face. In the new creation neither the road nor the robbers will be there, and the wounded will be healed. The hurt will have been mended by the One whose mercy the parable only sketches.

sermon.title: The Good Samaritan: On Love
sermon.why: Keller expounds the parable of the Good Samaritan from Luke 10, showing that love is what we were built for and that Jesus is the ultimate neighbor who rescues us at His own cost. A faithful, Christ-centered handling of this movement's central parable.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus tell the seventy-two to rejoice?

options.text: That their names are written in heaven, rather than merely that demons submitted to them.
options.note: Luke 10:20 redirects their joy from power to their secure standing in grace.

options.text: That they had authority to tread on snakes and scorpions.
options.note: He did grant this authority, but told them the deeper joy is their names in heaven, not their power.

options.text: That they had become more important than other disciples.
options.note: The point is grace, not status; nothing here elevates them over others.

options.text: That they would be spared all future hardship.
options.note: He sends them as lambs among wolves; the promise is heavenly security, not an easy life.

quiz.q: What was the lawyer trying to do when he asked, who is my neighbor?

options.text: To justify himself by narrowing whom he was obligated to love.
options.note: Luke 10:29 says he asked wanting to justify himself.

options.text: To genuinely learn the limits of the command out of humble curiosity.
options.note: The wording sounds like a sincere question, but the text says he was seeking to justify himself.

options.text: To trap Jesus into denying the law of Moses.
options.note: He came to test Jesus, but this particular question aimed at self-justification, not at contradicting the law.

options.text: To confess that he had failed to love his neighbor.
options.note: The opposite: he was defending himself, not confessing failure.

quiz.q: What moved the Samaritan to help the wounded man?

options.text: He had compassion, a gut-deep mercy, and acted at his own cost.
options.note: Luke 10:33-35 shows compassion leading to costly, practical care.

options.text: He bandaged the man's wounds and paid the innkeeper.
options.note: True actions, but they flowed from the compassion that first moved him; the deeds are the fruit, the mercy the root.

options.text: He felt obligated because the man was a fellow Samaritan.
options.note: The wounded man was a Jew; the Samaritan crossed enmity, not kinship, to help.

options.text: He hoped to be repaid and honored for his trouble.
options.note: He paid out of his own pocket and promised to cover more, seeking no reward.

quiz.q: What did Jesus mean by the one thing necessary that Mary had chosen?

options.text: Sitting at His feet to hear His word, the good portion that cannot be taken away.
options.note: Luke 10:42 commends Mary's attentive listening as the one necessary thing.

options.text: That quiet is better than serving guests.
options.note: It is not stillness in general but hearing Jesus that is praised; service is good when it flows from that.

options.text: That Martha was wrong to welcome Jesus into her home.
options.note: Martha's welcome was good; her anxious distraction, not her hospitality, was the problem.

options.text: That practical work does not matter to Jesus at all.
options.note: Jesus values service, but it must not crowd out listening to Him.

quiz.q: How does the Good Samaritan point to Christ?

options.text: As the despised outsider who rescues the helpless at His own cost and promises to return, He mirrors Jesus who saves us and will come again.
options.note: The mercy commanded is the very mercy Christ shows in coming to save the ruined.

options.text: He shows that we should be kind to people in need.
options.note: True and central to the parable, but it also pictures the saving mercy of Christ Himself.

options.text: He teaches that only Samaritans can be saved.
options.note: The Samaritan is the hero of mercy, not a claim about who alone is saved.

options.text: He proves that religious leaders are always right.
options.note: The priest and Levite pass by; the parable exposes religion without mercy.

questions: Jesus told the seventy-two to rejoice most that their names are written in heaven. When your week goes well or badly, where does your joy actually rest?
The lawyer wanted to know how little love he could get away with. Where are you tempted to draw a line around who counts as your neighbor?
A priest and a Levite saw the wounded man and passed by. Who is the person you are most tempted to cross to the other side of the road to avoid?
The Samaritan's mercy cost him time, oil, wine, money, and a promise to return. What would costly, not merely convenient, mercy look like for you this week?
Martha was worried and upset about many things, while Mary sat and listened. What good and busy things are crowding out your time at Jesus' feet?

translationNotes.note: Seventy-two follows many early manuscripts; others read seventy, as reflected in the BSB footnote. The number may echo the seventy or seventy-two nations of Genesis 10, hinting that the mission is ultimately for the whole world.
The lawyer weaves together Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18. Jesus affirms this summary of the law, then presses its meaning home through the parable.
Two denarii represented roughly two days' wages for a laborer, enough for an extended stay at the inn; the Samaritan also pledges to cover any further cost, underscoring the generosity of his mercy.
